source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

coverage.syllabusAssignment: Separation of Powers; Federal/State/Private Nondelegation; Article III & Seventh Amendment
coverage.status: Textbook excerpt supplied; check later assigned 2026 supplements separately

topics.title: § 7.1 — Political Branches: Separation of Powers (pp. 417–418)
topics.description: Separation of powers, checks and balances, formalism versus functionalism; state variations.

entries.title: Separation of powers
entries.summary: The Constitution assigns specialized powers to the legislative, executive, and judicial branches, though federal agencies commonly combine delegated rulemaking, adjudicatory, and enforcement responsibilities.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government powers are separated, but agencies routinely do more than one type of governmental work.
entries.legalExplanation: The separation-of-powers framework raises questions about whether and how a branch may transfer functions or interfere with another branch's constitutionally assigned work.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examApplication: Identify which branch holds the constitutional power, how the agency exercises it, and which branch is attempting to control it.

entries.title: Checks and balances
entries.summary: Each governmental branch must be able to resist encroachment and curb arbitrary action by the others.
entries.laymanExplanation: The branches are separated but must also be able to check each other.
entries.legalExplanation: Legislative, executive, and judicial oversight of agencies both implements and potentially threatens constitutional checks and balances.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Formalist approach
entries.summary: A formalist separation-of-powers analysis uses categorical boundaries and bright-line limits on branch functions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Ask which branch constitutionally owns the function, not whether crossing the line seems useful.
entries.legalExplanation: Formal analysis tends to enforce textual or structural prohibitions without open-ended balancing of costs or benefits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Functionalist approach
entries.summary: A functionalist separation-of-powers analysis weighs practical consequences, degrees of intrusion, and competing institutional interests.
entries.laymanExplanation: Ask how much a proposed arrangement interferes with another branch and whether that interference is justified.
entries.legalExplanation: Balancing and context-specific inquiry predominate, unlike formalism's categorical rules.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examTrap: Neither style governs every separation-of-powers problem; Supreme Court cases mix approaches.

entries.title: State constitutional agency structures
entries.summary: States may constitutionalize agencies or elect executive officials directly, altering the usual accountability and oversight relationships.
entries.laymanExplanation: State agencies sometimes have their own constitutional status and officials elected independently of the governor.
entries.legalExplanation: State separation-of-powers disputes require state-specific constitutional provisions, elected-office arrangements, and precedent, not reflexive federal analogy.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

topics.title: § 7.2.1 — Federal Nondelegation (pp. 418–440)
topics.description: Federal intelligible principle and evolution from Field through Gundy, with assigned Benzene and Gundy excerpts, interpretive avoidance, and problem.

entries.title: Federal nondelegation doctrine
entries.summary: Congress may delegate substantial implementation discretion but cannot transfer the legislative power vested in Congress by Article I without constitutionally adequate limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress must make the law's basic policy choices, but agencies can fill in many practical details.
entries.legalExplanation: The familiar federal formulation asks whether Congress supplied an intelligible principle to guide the delegate; the reading contrasts formalist and practical justifications.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examApplication: Identify statute, delegee, scope of power, articulated policies/standards, regulatory context, and controlling precedents.

entries.title: Two theories behind nondelegation
entries.summary: Strict separation-of-powers arguments oppose transfer of legislative power; checks-and-balances arguments tolerate some delegation subject to meaningful statutory limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: One view says Congress cannot give away legislative power; another says it must set ground rules when giving agencies discretion.
entries.legalExplanation: The text distinguishes absolute non-transfer from an intelligible-principle approach that limits discretion.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Marshall Field & Co. v. Clark (1892) — factual contingency
entries.summary: The Supreme Court upheld contingent tariff authority: Congress selected a legal consequence triggered by presidential findings about unequal foreign tariffs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress set the tariff consequence and let the President determine when foreign conditions triggered it.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court characterized presidential action as finding a contingency under a law Congress had enacted, though the textbook questions the accuracy of describing the substantial discretion as mere fact-finding.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Explained and excerpted in casebook narrative, not a complete assigned opinion
entries.facts: Congress authorized increased duties and suspended favorable tariffs upon the President's determination that a foreign nation imposed unequal or unreasonable tariffs.
entries.issue: Did allowing the President to determine when Congress's tariff consequence applied impermissibly delegate legislative power?
entries.reasoning: Congress enacted the consequence and allowed the President to ascertain when the statutory contingency existed.
entries.rule: An executive determination of factual conditions triggering a legislatively chosen consequence may be delegated.
entries.examTrap: Field's characterization is contested by the textbook because determining foreign tariffs and retaliation entails significant policy judgment.

entries.title: J.W. Hampton — intelligible principle
entries.summary: Delegation is generally permissible when Congress lays down an intelligible principle guiding the official authorized to act.
entries.laymanExplanation: A broad agency task is generally acceptable if Congress states the policy or standard guiding it.
entries.legalExplanation: J.W. Hampton Jr. & Co. v. United States (1928) gave the durable federal nondelegation formula.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examTrap: Intelligible principle is historically lenient and should not be confused with Gorsuch's noncontrolling proposal in Gundy.

entries.title: Broad early standards often upheld
entries.summary: Standards such as preventing unfair methods of competition and regulating the airwaves for public convenience, interest, or necessity were upheld notwithstanding vagueness.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts accepted surprisingly open-ended agency instructions before the New Deal.
entries.legalExplanation: The cited authorities illustrate permissive application of Hampton to regulatory programs.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Panama Refining Co. v. Ryan (1935) — no governing standard
entries.summary: The Supreme Court invalidated NIRA § 9(c), which allowed the President to prohibit interstate transport of oil produced contrary to state production restrictions without a sufficient federal standard.
entries.laymanExplanation: The President could choose whether to ban 'hot oil' without Congress telling him the conditions for that choice.
entries.legalExplanation: The majority found no policy or limiting rule for the critical exercise of presidential discretion; Cardozo dissented based on the statute's context.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Substantial excerpts and narrative in the assigned reading
entries.facts: Congress authorized a presidential ban on interstate shipment of oil produced above Texas's limits during an oil overproduction crisis.
entries.issue: Did NIRA § 9(c) adequately constrain presidential authority to impose the ban?
entries.reasoning: Congress specified neither the criteria for choosing a ban nor a sufficiently defined policy directing that choice.
entries.rule: A delegation without a congressional policy or standard governing the decision may violate Article I.
entries.examApplication: Compare the open-ended emergency discretion to Field's contingent-tariff structure.

entries.title: A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935)
entries.summary: The Court invalidated NIRA § 3's open-ended grant to adopt industry-wide fair-competition codes with criminal consequences and inadequate standards or procedures.
entries.laymanExplanation: The President could remake economic rules for many industries without sufficient congressional direction.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court emphasized unbounded breadth, the lack of defined regulatory standards and procedures, and the role of interested businesses in writing binding codes; Cardozo characterized the grant as an excessive roving commission.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Detailed narrative and excerpts in assigned reading
entries.facts: NIRA authorized presidential fair-competition codes controlling wages, prices, hours, and production; a poultry wholesaler was convicted under a code.
entries.issue: Did Congress constitutionally delegate adoption of broad binding fair-competition codes?
entries.reasoning: The scheme reached across the economy without intelligible policy limitations and involved private producers in shaping enforceable rules.
entries.rule: Unbounded authority to adopt industry codes based on undefined fair competition was an invalid delegation.
entries.examTrap: The New Deal emergency did not itself save the delegation.

entries.title: Yakus v. United States (1944) — flexible standards
entries.summary: The Court upheld World War II price controls using the general standard 'generally fair and equitable,' rejecting demands for maximal specificity during complex emergency regulation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress could instruct an administrator to control wartime prices under a broad fairness standard.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court emphasized flexibility, overall congressional anti-inflation policy, statutory directions concerning prior prices, and the possibility of meaningful judicial review.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Excerpted and explained in reading
entries.facts: A seller challenged conviction for exceeding an administratively established beef price ceiling under the Emergency Price Control Act.
entries.issue: Was the wartime price delegation unconstitutional?
entries.reasoning: Congress need not adopt the least-discretionary method where flexibility is necessary and the governing policy provides judicially discernible bounds.
entries.rule: Broad standards can suffice in a complex regulatory program when legislative policy and reviewable limits exist.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish Schechter/Panama's absence of policy standards from an articulated anti-inflation program.

entries.title: Historical status of federal nondelegation cases
entries.summary: The casebook identifies Panama Refining and Schechter as the two 1935 Supreme Court invalidations of federal statutory delegations and describes later doctrine as generally permissive.
entries.laymanExplanation: For decades the Supreme Court upheld very broad delegations, with the 1935 cases as exceptional invalidations.
entries.legalExplanation: This is the reading's historical account through publication; evaluate later assigned decisions separately.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Industrial Union Department v. American Petroleum Institute (Benzene) (1980)
entries.summary: A four-Justice plurality construed OSHA's authority to require a threshold finding of significant risk of material health impairment before setting a toxic exposure limit; it invalidated the benzene standard under that interpretation.
entries.laymanExplanation: OSHA had to identify a significant worker risk before imposing the chosen benzene limit, rather than requiring the lowest feasible exposure to any possible risk.
entries.legalExplanation: The plurality adopted a narrowing construction to avoid an arguably sweeping, standardless delegation; Rehnquist concurred on nondelegation grounds, Powell favored cost-benefit analysis, and Marshall dissented.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.facts: OSHA reduced permissible benzene exposure to 1 ppm under a feasible-safety reading despite insufficient findings establishing danger below 10 ppm.
entries.issue: Did the Occupational Safety and Health Act permit OSHA to set this standard without establishing significant risk, and did the agency follow the statutory limit?
entries.holding: The benzene standard was set aside; the plurality required an antecedent significant-risk finding.
entries.reasoning: Without a significant-risk threshold, the agency's interpretation potentially gave it sweeping control over workplace substances despite minimal harm evidence; constitutional avoidance supported the narrower statutory reading.
entries.rule: Under the Benzene plurality, OSHA must find a significant risk of material health impairment before regulating toxic exposure through the relevant standard.
entries.exam: Separate plurality statutory interpretation from Rehnquist's separate argument that the delegation itself was invalid.
entries.examApplication: Compare a public-health statute's articulated threshold with an agency's reliance on any imaginable risk.
entries.examTrap: Do not attribute Rehnquist's constitutional invalidation position to the four-Justice plurality.

entries.title: Benzene — Rehnquist nondelegation concurrence
entries.summary: Rehnquist believed § 6(b)(5) failed to resolve fundamental policy tradeoffs and did not give OSHA an intelligible standard; Congress had to make the core life-versus-cost decision.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress cannot avoid a hard political choice by telling an agency merely to do what is feasible.
entries.legalExplanation: He articulated democratic accountability, agency guidance, and judicial review as three nondelegation objectives; his constitutional position was not the plurality's holding.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Benzene — Marshall dissent and Cotton Dust
entries.summary: Marshall argued feasible worker protection was a sufficiently definite congressional choice; the following year's Cotton Dust decision upheld OSHA's statutory interpretation of 'feasible.'
entries.laymanExplanation: The dissent argued that Congress had chosen to protect workers as far as feasible, even where risks couldn't be precisely measured.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrasts with Rehnquist's nondelegation objection and the plurality's significant-risk construction.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Gundy v. United States, 588 U.S. 128 (2019)
entries.summary: The Court upheld SORNA authority for the Attorney General to specify application of sex-offender registration requirements to pre-Act offenders, reading the statute as permitting limited timing and implementation discretion.
entries.laymanExplanation: The Attorney General could work out how quickly to register people convicted before the statute, not choose whether to apply the law to them at all.
entries.legalExplanation: Kagan's opinion relied on SORNA's purpose, surrounding provisions, and implementation problem to identify an intelligible principle; Alito concurred in judgment while expressing openness to revisiting the doctrine.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.facts: Herman Gundy, convicted before SORNA, failed to register after release and challenged the Attorney General's authority to specify SORNA's application to pre-Act offenders.
entries.issue: Did 34 U.S.C. § 20913(d) delegate legislative power without an intelligible principle?
entries.reasoning: Properly construed, Congress had made the policy choice for registration and left the Attorney General transitional implementation decisions, bounded by feasibility and timing.
entries.rule: Under Gundy's controlling judgment, a contextual, implementation-focused reading of the SORNA delegation satisfied the established intelligible-principle standard.
entries.exam: Identify Kagan's statutory narrowing, Alito's vote for the judgment, and Gorsuch's competing proposed approach.
entries.examApplication: Ask if the agency chooses whether the policy applies or merely works out implementation details.
entries.examTrap: Do not state that Gorsuch's dissent is the binding nondelegation test.

entries.title: Gundy — Gorsuch dissent's three permitted delegations
entries.summary: Gorsuch would allow Congress to let officials fill details after Congress makes policy, ascertain facts triggering law, or exercise powers independently granted to another branch, but not legislate private conduct.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies can implement Congress's choices, but cannot make Congress's fundamental policy choice themselves.
entries.legalExplanation: Gorsuch, joined by Roberts and Thomas, criticized the lax intelligible-principle formula and SORNA's alleged transfer of criminal rulemaking power.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.elements: 1. Fill in statutory details. 2. Find facts triggering Congress's rule. 3. Exercise another branch's independent constitutional power.
entries.examTrap: This is a dissent, not the majority's governing standard.

entries.title: Gundy — Alito concurrence and future reconsideration
entries.summary: Alito voted to uphold the delegation under existing doctrine but indicated willingness to reconsider the approach with a majority.
entries.laymanExplanation: He applied the old test in this case while remaining open to changing it later.
entries.legalExplanation: Kavanaugh did not participate; later commentary discussed possible reconsideration.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Debate over enforcing nondelegation more strictly
entries.summary: Proponents emphasize congressional accountability and prevent agencies or influential legislators from making hidden policy choices; critics stress Congress's institutional limits and the risks of subjective judicial invalidation.
entries.laymanExplanation: More restrictive delegation can force Congress to take responsibility, but may make complex regulation and politically difficult compromises harder.
entries.legalExplanation: Reading contrasts Schoenbrod/Rao with Stewart/Mashaw and critiques both legislative blame shifting and judicially managed specificity.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Nondelegation as a statutory-interpretation canon
entries.summary: Courts sometimes narrowly construe broad delegations to avoid constitutional concerns, rather than strike down the statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: A judge may read an ambiguous agency grant more narrowly to keep it constitutional.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading links Benzene and Gundy to avoidance arguments but flags concerns that judicial narrowing can become rewriting Congress's chosen delegation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examApplication: Analyze textual support for a narrower construction before addressing constitutional invalidation.

entries.title: Judicial review and delegation
entries.summary: Meaningful judicial review can constrain exercises of delegated authority and reassure courts that agencies operate within congressional limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts can check whether agencies stay inside their delegated powers, so broad delegation may pose less risk.
entries.legalExplanation: Touby interpreted an apparent review bar to allow challenges in a criminal prosecution; absence of review can exacerbate nondelegation concerns.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Sunstein's nondelegation canons
entries.summary: Interpretive clear-statement rules can reserve contested choices, such as retroactive regulation and displacement of state law, for Congress unless Congress clearly authorizes agency action.
entries.laymanExplanation: For sensitive policy decisions, courts may demand especially clear permission before an agency acts.
entries.legalExplanation: This is a scholarly method of protecting nondelegation values through statutory interpretation, distinct from constitutional invalidation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

topics.title: §§ 7.2.2–7.2.3 — State & Private Delegation (pp. 440–451)
topics.description: State standards/safeguards, assigned Thygesen, private delegation oversight, privatization, and state budget problem.

entries.title: State nondelegation standards
entries.summary: Many states enforce nondelegation more strictly than federal courts and demand substantive policy or statutory standards, although judicial approaches vary by jurisdiction.
entries.laymanExplanation: A state agency may need clearer legislative instructions than a federal agency would.
entries.legalExplanation: State constitutions often contain express separation-of-powers clauses; the casebook discusses strong, moderate, and safeguards-oriented state tests.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examApplication: Identify the state's constitutional text and local nondelegation framework before importing federal Hampton doctrine.

entries.title: Thygesen v. Callahan, 385 N.E.2d 699 (Ill. 1979)
entries.summary: Illinois struck down authority to set maximum currency-exchange rates because Congress's state counterpart specified regulated parties but did not identify the harm or adequate means guiding the rate decisions.
entries.laymanExplanation: The legislature told a regulator who to regulate but failed to explain what problem the price caps should solve.
entries.legalExplanation: The court followed Stofer's three-part standards inquiry and held that vague reasonableness did not supply the missing statutory policy.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.facts: Illinois authorized its financial institutions director to set maximum charges for check cashing and money orders under its APA, without stating the particular harm or meaningful policy standard for those maximums.
entries.issue: Did the Illinois Currency Exchange Act supply sufficient intelligible standards for the director's rate regulation?
entries.holding: No; the rate-setting delegation was unconstitutional.
entries.reasoning: The statute identified the affected exchange businesses and activities but failed to express the harm to remedy or guiding means; general requirements of reasonable rulemaking were insufficient.
entries.rule: Under the Illinois Stofer framework, a delegation should identify regulated persons and activities, the harm to be prevented, and the general means by which the agency may address it.
entries.exam: Use the three prongs individually rather than treating a general reasonableness requirement as automatically sufficient.
entries.examApplication: Explicitly identify the absent harm and any asserted statutory objectives; compare related provisions and procedural safeguards.
entries.examTrap: Illinois did not treat notice-and-comment procedures alone as a substitute for missing substantive standards.

entries.title: Stofer three-part state delegation test
entries.summary: Illinois evaluates whether an enabling statute sufficiently identifies (1) regulated persons and activities, (2) harm to be prevented, and (3) general means available to prevent it.
entries.laymanExplanation: The legislature must say who is regulated, why, and generally how.
entries.legalExplanation: Stofer's test structures Thygesen's analysis and demands more than a generic direction to act reasonably.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examApplication: Organize an Illinois state nondelegation answer under all three prongs.

entries.title: Standards versus safeguards in state nondelegation
entries.summary: Some states look to procedural safeguards and appeal rights instead of demanding detailed legislative standards; federal Whitman doctrine rejects procedure as a substitute for an intelligible principle.
entries.laymanExplanation: A law may be accepted because agency procedures and appeals protect people, even if policy instructions are broad, depending on the state.
entries.legalExplanation: Warren (Oregon) and Barry & Barry (Washington) emphasize safeguards; Askew (Florida) insists that the legislature not surrender major policy choices.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Do stricter nondelegation rules change legislative detail?
entries.summary: Empirical studies summarized in the textbook report weak or absent links between aggressive state nondelegation review and more specific statutes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Striking down broad statutes may not actually make legislatures write more detailed laws.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading identifies competing interpretations of the evidence; treat this as scholarly context, not a constitutional test.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: New York sugary-drink portion cap — policy choice reserved to legislature
entries.summary: New York's highest court invalidated a Board of Health rule limiting sugary drinks larger than 16 ounces, concluding that officials had made fundamental balancing decisions outside delegated authority.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency cannot use general public-health authority to independently choose a major compromise between public health and economic policy when the legislature reserved it.
entries.legalExplanation: Majority considered legislative-versus-agency policymaking; dissent emphasized ordinary agency cost-benefit tradeoffs.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in notes, no full opinion reproduced

entries.title: State incorporation of evolving federal law
entries.summary: State law sometimes adopts current or future federal standards; courts disagree whether this improperly transfers state legislative power.
entries.laymanExplanation: A state may use federal rules as a shortcut, but courts disagree when future federal changes can automatically change state law.
entries.legalExplanation: Michigan's Taylor accepts independently significant federal decisions as triggers; Oklahoma City rejects unrestricted reliance on federal bureaucrats to decide local wage policy.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Private nondelegation
entries.summary: Legislative transfers of binding governmental authority to private actors raise heightened concerns about self-interest, lack of political control, and absence of public-law procedures.
entries.laymanExplanation: A private business should not get unchecked lawmaking power over competitors.
entries.legalExplanation: Constitutional scrutiny focuses on binding control, conflicts, public supervision, judicial review, and whether governmental officials can reject private proposals.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Carter v. Carter Coal Co. (1936) — improper private delegation
entries.summary: The Court struck down binding labor rules made by a majority of miners and operators over nonconsenting competitors, emphasizing self-interested private control.
entries.laymanExplanation: Businesses and workers cannot be allowed to impose binding terms on others merely by voting among themselves.
entries.legalExplanation: The central concern was coercive authority vested in private persons whose interests may oppose those regulated.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in notes, not full opinion

entries.title: Currin v. Wallace (1939) — private approval as trigger
entries.summary: A regulatory program may condition the operation of government-made rules on a vote by affected private parties.
entries.laymanExplanation: Private parties may decide whether a government rule becomes operative, without themselves writing the binding rule.
entries.legalExplanation: The government retained substantive policymaking, and the private vote served as a contingency.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in notes only

entries.title: Sunshine Anthracite Coal Co. v. Adkins (1940) — public control
entries.summary: Private organizations may propose standards when politically accountable government officials retain supervisory authority to approve or override them.
entries.laymanExplanation: A private group can suggest standards if the government has the final say.
entries.legalExplanation: Meaningful public review mitigates dangers of private delegation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in notes only

entries.title: FINRA private oversight and SEC review
entries.summary: FINRA's rules and disciplinary actions are subject to SEC review, providing an important public check; the excerpt notes a later challenge to immediate expulsion without awaiting SEC supervision.
entries.laymanExplanation: Private financial regulators need government review when they wield coercive power.
entries.legalExplanation: Todd & Co. upheld a model with SEC control; Alpine Securities raised a question where enforcement preceded that review.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examTrap: Private implementation with genuine government control differs from independent, binding private lawmaking.

entries.title: Horseracing Integrity and Safety Authority — circuit conflict in reading
entries.summary: The Fifth Circuit viewed private horseracing oversight as inadequately supervised as to enforcement even after amendments strengthened FTC review of rulemaking; other circuits disagreed.
entries.laymanExplanation: A government supervisor's power over rules may not resolve whether private investigators and adjudicators are adequately controlled.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook describes Horsemen's I and II and opposing Sixth/Eighth Circuit outcomes; it forecasts further Supreme Court consideration, so treat that forecast as dated context.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Cases summarized in notes, not reproduced opinions
entries.examTrap: Do not treat casebook predictions about future Supreme Court outcomes as a holding.

entries.title: Privatization and inherently governmental functions
entries.summary: Contracting out government work raises accountability, procedural, ethical, and effectiveness questions; certain inherently governmental decisions cannot simply be transferred to contractors.
entries.laymanExplanation: Contractors may provide services but should not automatically make sovereign decisions about prosecution or war.
entries.legalExplanation: The exact boundary of inherently governmental functions is contested; the excerpt mentions detention and prisons as difficult examples.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: State private-delegation scrutiny
entries.summary: States may scrutinize private delegations more heavily than public ones, considering conflict of interest and public control.
entries.laymanExplanation: A private regulator acting in its own interest can face stricter review.
entries.legalExplanation: Texas Boll Weevil supplies an example involving regulatory and assessment power backed by coercive sanctions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Federal delegation to state actors
entries.summary: Congress must affirmatively authorize an agency's transfer of federal decisionmaking powers to state institutions; the federal agency cannot simply delegate those duties on its own.
entries.laymanExplanation: Cooperative federalism is possible, but an agency cannot invent its own subdelegation to a state government.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes cite U.S. Telecom. Ass'n v. FCC for the principle that executive subdelegation requires congressional authorization.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Texas Boll Weevil Eradication Foundation v. Lewellen — private delegation
entries.summary: Texas invalidated a privately controlled cotton-pest scheme that allowed interested farmers to impose assessments, regulate, and sanction others with inadequate public oversight.
entries.laymanExplanation: Cotton growers on a private board could impose costs and sanctions on other growers despite conflicts and weak government checks.
entries.legalExplanation: Factors included weak government supervision, financial interests, criminal enforcement, few standards, wide scope, and lack of competence safeguards.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in notes only
entries.examApplication: Apply control, conflict-of-interest, scope, penalty, competence, and procedural safeguards to a private regulation hypothetical.

topics.title: § 7.3.1 — Article III Limits on Agency Adjudication (pp. 451–454)
topics.description: Public versus private rights; Crowell, Northern Pipeline, Thomas, Schor, Oil States, Stern.

entries.title: Article III and administrative adjudication
entries.summary: Article III vests federal judicial power in judges with life tenure and salary protection; assigning adjudication to agencies implicates this protection and the public-rights exception.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some disputes must be decided by independent Article III judges, while others can be handled initially by agencies.
entries.legalExplanation: The public/private rights framework, agency expertise, and judicial review affect when non-Article III tribunals may resolve matters.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examApplication: Identify nature/origin of claim, claimant/defendant, whether dispute is part of a federal regulatory scheme, and Article III review.

entries.title: Public rights versus private rights
entries.summary: Public rights often concern governmental regulatory entitlements or sovereign prerogatives; private rights typically include traditional common-law liabilities between private parties.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government benefits, patents, or regulatory matters may be public rights; a private tort lawsuit is more likely a private right.
entries.legalExplanation: The Supreme Court's formulations have varied. A public-rights label cannot automatically be applied merely because Congress passes a statute.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examTrap: Jarkesy looks to the substance of a fraud action, not merely the presence of the SEC as plaintiff.

entries.title: Crowell v. Benson (1932) — administrative workers' compensation
entries.summary: The Supreme Court upheld administrative resolution of a compensation claim involving private rights where Article III courts retained independent authority over legal and certain fundamental fact questions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies could initially decide workers' compensation while federal judges kept important reviewing powers.
entries.legalExplanation: Historically the Court distinguished jurisdictional/constitutional facts from ordinary facts; later decisions retreated from the special facts doctrine.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Described in reading rather than fully reproduced
entries.facts: A worker claimed statutory compensation for injury on navigable waters in an employee relationship.
entries.issue: Can an administrative body adjudicate a private employment-based liability claim consistently with Article III?
entries.holding: Yes, with a substantial reviewing role for Article III courts.
entries.reasoning: Congress may assign public rights to agencies and some private-rights fact finding when courts decide law and fundamental jurisdictional and constitutional questions independently.
entries.rule: Administrative factfinding with meaningful judicial control may coexist with Article III, though aspects of Crowell's facts doctrine were later abandoned.

entries.title: Northern Pipeline v. Marathon Pipe Line (1982) — bankruptcy contract suit
entries.summary: A non-Article III bankruptcy judge could not finally resolve a traditional state-law breach-of-contract dispute under the broad statutory bankruptcy jurisdiction then enacted.
entries.laymanExplanation: A bankruptcy judge without Article III protections cannot automatically decide an ordinary private contract case.
entries.legalExplanation: Brennan's plurality emphasized private rights; the concurrence reached a narrower contract-specific result.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Summarized; complete opinion not reproduced
entries.facts: Bankruptcy legislation gave non-Article III bankruptcy judges authority to decide a breach-of-contract dispute.
entries.issue: May Congress assign full final adjudicatory authority over that private-rights claim to bankruptcy judges?
entries.holding: The challenged broad grant was unconstitutional.
entries.reasoning: The dispute involved a traditional private contract claim without an adequate Article III basis for final adjudication.
entries.rule: Traditional private-rights disputes can limit final adjudicatory authority by non-Article III tribunals.
entries.examTrap: Distinguish the four-Justice plurality's sweeping reasoning from the narrower concurrence.

entries.title: Thomas v. Union Carbide Agricultural Products (1985)
entries.summary: The Court permitted administrative arbitration of data-compensation rights between pesticide registrants where the claims were closely integrated with a federal registration scheme.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency-associated process can decide a dispute between companies if Congress created it as part of a complex regulatory system.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court viewed the apparent private rights as tightly integrated with the statutory federal regulatory program.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in reading, not reproduced

entries.title: CFTC v. Schor (1986) — limited common-law counterclaims
entries.summary: The Court upheld the CFTC's adjudication of a limited broker counterclaim under state law ancillary to a congressionally authorized reparations proceeding.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency can sometimes decide a small related private-law counterclaim while resolving a specialized regulatory dispute.
entries.legalExplanation: A functional inquiry emphasized the narrow nature of the additional claim and modest intrusion on Article III courts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in reading, not reproduced

entries.title: Oil States v. Greene's Energy Group (2018) — patent public rights
entries.summary: PTAB review of patent validity was constitutionally assignable to the agency because issuing patents is a governmental public-rights matter, even when two private actors dispute validity.
entries.laymanExplanation: Patent validity can be reconsidered by a patent agency because the patent comes from a government grant.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court characterized inter partes review as reconsideration of the original public grant, not necessarily a private damages suit.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in reading, not reproduced

entries.title: Stern v. Marshall (2011) — traditional tort counterclaim
entries.summary: A non-Article III bankruptcy judge could not finally adjudicate a tortious-interference counterclaim that was a traditional state-law private right and not essential to resolving a creditor claim.
entries.laymanExplanation: A bankruptcy court cannot decide every ordinary state-law tort dispute simply because it appears as a bankruptcy counterclaim.
entries.legalExplanation: The majority distinguished cases involving claims created by federal regulatory law or necessary to a limited regulatory scheme.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in reading, not reproduced

topics.title: § 7.3.2 — Seventh Amendment and Jarkesy (pp. 454–466)
topics.description: Atlas Roofing, Tull, Granfinanciera, assigned SEC v. Jarkesy majority and separate opinions, remedy distinctions, advertising problem.

entries.title: Seventh Amendment jury-trial protection
entries.summary: A federal civil jury right attaches to suits analogous to traditional common-law legal claims; legal remedies—especially punitive monetary penalties—carry substantial weight.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a case is basically a common-law legal suit for punishment or money penalties, a jury may be required.
entries.legalExplanation: Courts assess both the historical nature of the cause of action and the remedy, while accounting for the public-rights exception.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examApplication: Analyze the claim and requested relief first, then whether the public-rights exception justifies agency adjudication.

entries.title: Atlas Roofing v. OSHRC (1977) — novel public rights penalties
entries.summary: The Court held the Seventh Amendment did not require juries in administrative proceedings imposing civil penalties for new OSHA duties unknown to common law.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency can impose civil penalties to enforce novel workplace safety obligations without a jury.
entries.legalExplanation: Congress created a new statutory public-rights regulatory obligation and assigned specialized enforcement to the agency.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in reading, not full opinion
entries.facts: Employers faced OSHA statutory workplace standards enforced by administrative civil money penalties.
entries.issue: Did the Seventh Amendment require a jury in the agency's civil-penalty case?
entries.reasoning: The claims enforced novel public-rights duties rather than familiar common-law causes of action.
entries.rule: The Seventh Amendment does not necessarily require juries for administrative enforcement of newly created public-rights duties.
entries.examTrap: Jarkesy later distinguished but expressly did not overrule Atlas Roofing.

entries.title: Tull v. United States (1987) — civil penalty in federal court
entries.summary: A defendant sued in federal court for Clean Water Act civil penalties had a jury right as to liability but not calculation of penalty amount.
entries.laymanExplanation: A court suit seeking civil punishment may require a jury on whether the defendant violated the law.
entries.legalExplanation: Tull distinguished liability jury determination from judicial calculation of civil penalty size.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in reading, not full opinion

entries.title: Granfinanciera v. Nordberg (1989) — fraudulent conveyance
entries.summary: A bankruptcy trustee's statutory fraudulent-transfer action was analogous to a historical suit at law and triggered a jury right despite assignment to a non-Article III bankruptcy tribunal.
entries.laymanExplanation: Putting a familiar fraudulent-transfer money claim into a bankruptcy statute does not remove the jury right.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court emphasized the substance of the private legal claim and rejected relabeling as a means to eliminate the Seventh Amendment.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in reading, not full opinion
entries.examApplication: Ask whether the statutory claim closely tracks an established common-law legal cause and whether the remedy is legal.

entries.title: SEC v. Jarkesy, 603 U.S. 109 (2024)
entries.summary: The SEC cannot compel an in-house administrative proceeding without a civil jury where it seeks punitive civil penalties for securities fraud closely resembling common-law fraud; the public-rights exception does not apply.
entries.laymanExplanation: If the SEC seeks to punish someone for securities fraud through civil penalties, the defendant is entitled to an Article III jury trial.
entries.legalExplanation: The majority focused on punitive monetary relief and common-law fraud analogies, not the claim's statutory label or SEC's presence; it distinguished Atlas Roofing and did not reach other constitutional challenges.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.facts: The SEC pursued Jarkesy and Patriot28 in an administrative ALJ proceeding for securities fraud, imposed $300,000 in civil penalties along with other sanctions, and defended its choice of forum.
entries.issue: Does the Seventh Amendment require an Article III jury when the SEC seeks civil penalties for fraud closely analogous to common-law fraud?
entries.holding: Yes. The constitutional jury right applies and the public-rights exception does not justify the SEC's in-house penalty adjudication.
entries.reasoning: Civil penalties punish and deter rather than merely restore the status quo; securities antifraud claims replicate historical common-law fraud; Congress cannot eliminate jury rights by labeling a traditional legal claim as administrative or statutory.
entries.rule: When a federal agency seeks punitive civil penalties for a cause of action substantively analogous to a traditional common-law suit, a jury right may prevent administrative final adjudication under the Seventh Amendment.
entries.exam: Distinguish majority Seventh Amendment holding from Gorsuch's broader Article III/due-process concurrence and Sotomayor's dissent. Identify remedy as especially important.
entries.examApplication: Identify whether the claim resembles common-law fraud and whether the remedy is punitive civil penalties; compare Atlas Roofing and other public-rights programs.
entries.examTrap: Jarkesy did not resolve ALJ removal or general nondelegation; nor did it overrule Atlas Roofing or categorically ban administrative civil penalties.

entries.title: Jarkesy — Gorsuch concurrence
entries.summary: Gorsuch and Thomas argued more broadly that agency combination of prosecutor, judge, and jury roles raises Article III and due-process objections.
entries.laymanExplanation: The concurrence would protect courts and juries more broadly against agency adjudication.
entries.legalExplanation: These statements go beyond the majority's narrower Seventh Amendment ruling.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Jarkesy — Sotomayor dissent
entries.summary: Sotomayor, joined by Kagan and Jackson, argued that the Government may enforce public statutory obligations through agency civil penalties and warned of broad disruption to administrative enforcement.
entries.laymanExplanation: The dissent thought government regulatory cases should remain administrative even where they involve monetary penalties.
entries.legalExplanation: She emphasized the sovereign claimant, Congress's longstanding practice, and distinctions from court litigation and private-party bankruptcy fraud claims.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Jarkesy scope and unresolved questions in textbook notes
entries.summary: The reading suggests distinctions involving civil penalties, equitable orders, common-law analogs, and fraud against private investors versus the government; the majority did not decide every administrative penalty regime.
entries.laymanExplanation: The decision might be narrow, especially where an agency uses nonpunitive remedies or enforces entirely new statutory duties.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook's prospective considerations are not controlling holdings. Evaluate the remedy and source of substantive duty separately.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examTrap: Avoid saying civil monetary penalties in every agency proceeding are unconstitutional.

entries.title: Seventh Amendment does not bind state administrative tribunals
entries.summary: Federal Seventh Amendment civil-jury guarantees are not incorporated against states, though state constitutional jury provisions may independently protect defendants.
entries.laymanExplanation: A state agency's jury-trial rules depend on that state's constitution, not automatically the federal Seventh Amendment.
entries.legalExplanation: Some state courts historically followed Atlas Roofing-style public-rights analysis; reconsideration after Jarkesy is a distinct state-law question.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466

entries.title: Limits on criminal punishment by agencies
entries.summary: Agencies cannot impose criminal imprisonment or criminal fines as administrative punishment, although Congress may criminalize violation of valid regulations and courts may impose criminal sentences.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency can write certain legally binding rules, but sending someone to prison requires court proceedings.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading distinguishes agency civil penalties from court-imposed criminal sanctions and cites Wong Wing and Grimaud.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.examApplication: Separate administrative civil penalty authority from the judicial imposition of criminal punishment.

entries.title: McHugh v. Santa Monica Rent Control Board — remedies
entries.summary: California upheld administratively awarded restitution of excess rents, but rejected self-executing rent withholding and punitive damages under the state separation-of-powers framework.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency could order landlords to return overcharges, but not necessarily authorize immediate self-help or extra punitive payments.
entries.legalExplanation: The court examined regulatory necessity and meaningful judicial checking power for remedies traditionally associated with courts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466
entries.sourceRole: Described in notes only

problems.title: PHS Virus X emergency quarantine — Mary
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466 (pp. 439–440)
problems.prompt: Congress authorizes the Public Health Service Director to regulate public health emergencies, offers no standards or definition, and permits criminal penalties. After WHO declares Virus X a pandemic, the Director issues interim-final rules without prior notice and comment. Local public-health directors may quarantine residents of designated areas; violations can bring fines or one year in prison. A quarantine must be announced locally and in the Federal Register. Oak City announces a quarantine after cases are found. Mary knowingly drives to a neighboring city for groceries; following prosecution, the trial court rejects challenges to the regulations' procedure and substance and to the statute's nondelegation validity and sentences her to six months. Assess prospects for reversal on appeal; compare the Pennsylvania and Wisconsin emergency-measures cases in the assigned text.

problems.title: Madison budget commission — $600 million cuts
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466 (pp. 447)
problems.prompt: Madison's state constitution requires a balanced budget. The legislature empowers an executive Budget Commission to make cuts necessary to balance the current year's appropriations, requiring cuts to reduce deficits without impairing essential functions or harming the public interest. The Commission cuts $600 million, including housing for homeless families. Children who would have received housing challenge the appropriation cut; assume standing and justiciability. Evaluate the Commission action; cf. Chiles v. Children A–F.

problems.title: Federal Advertising Commission — Paragon and Invigorall
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), §§ 7.1–7.3, pp. 417–466 (pp. 465–466)
problems.prompt: A fictional federal deceptive-advertising law creates the Federal Advertising Commission (FAC) with authority for APA Type A hearings, cease-and-desist orders, disgorgement, and district-court civil-penalty suits; a later amendment authorizes civil penalties in agency proceedings. FAC alleges Paragon Corporation's Invigorall tonic advertising falsely suggests energizing medical benefits for ordinary consumers though only a small minority can benefit. After an ALJ hearing and commission approval, FAC orders the company to stop the ads and pay a $500,000 civil penalty. Paragon argues the nonjury agency proceeding violates the Seventh Amendment and Article III. Evaluate its appeal; cf. J.B. Williams and Reader's Digest.
